KEY MESSAGE 1...Scattered showers and thunderstorms return this evening
through Wednesday morning. Risk for a few strong to severe 
storms and heavy downpours. Localized flash flooding possible in
poor drainage areas. 

An upper level trough slowly pushes across eastern U.S./Canada today 
through Thursday with a several pieces of shortwave energy moving 
through the flow. At the surface, this will sweep a few frontal 
boundaries across the northeast as a surface low tracks across 
Quebec. This will support the return of unsettled weather with 
potential for strong storms and minor localized flash flooding 
tonight into Wednesday. A 40-50 kt LLJ with be the main player with 
the set-up, helping advect in richer moisture (dewpoints around 70F) 
with precipitable water values rising to 1.5-2.0"+ across southern 
New England this evening. Instability varies from marginal to 
moderate across high-resolution guidance with MU/SBCAPE values 800-
1500 J/kg. This is sufficient to support thunderstorm development if 
instability is available while aligning with an incoming shortwave. 
Model soundings do show hodographs supportive of stronger shear and 
helicity values in the 0-3 km layer. This environment will not only 
be support of heavy downpours, but also a strong to severe storm or 
two with damaging winds. Can't rule out the low risk of a brief 
"spin-up" given the supportive wind/shear profiles. 

Anomalous PWATs combined with warm cloud depths of 11,000-13,000+ ft 
allow for efficient rain processes and more importantly support 
heavy rainfall. As far as the QPF probs go, 18z guidance backed off 
a little with the probs of 1"+ and 2"+ overall, but it's just one 
run. We are still overall seeing a good signal for 24hr amounts 1"+ 
shown by the moderate to high probabilities (50-80%) especially 
along the south coast and Cape and Islands and low to moderate 
probabilities for 2"+ focused along the immediate south coast and 
Cape/Islands. 

The timeframe at which this falls will be the big factor for flash 
flooding potential. Given that embedded storms are possible, 
localized flash flooding is certainly a concern. The HREF PMM 
reflects this well with localized areas of 2"+ across western CT, RI 
and southeast MA, but also many streaks of 1-1.25" across the 
region. Slow storm motion will not be a concern with mid-level 
flow >30kts; however, there is a prominent LLJ suppling 
plentiful moisture upstream while steering storms consistently 
SW to NE. Training of heavier rain and thunderstorm may be 
possible as a result. The HREF probability of 1 hr precip 
exceeding 1 hr FFG reflects this well with higher probabilities 
in NJ and southern NY with low probs extending into western CT. 
There are a few spots of low probs across MA and RI 
tonight/early Wednesday. All this is pointing to is a lower 
probability of seeing widespread flash flood impacts. The HREF 
showing scattered low probabilities(< 20%) of >1.0"/hr rain 
rates mainly across portions of CT and moreso RI and southeast 
MA/Cape & Islands. So we'll have to keep an eye on localized 
minor flash flooding issues, especially in the more flashy areas
or urban/poor drainage areas (Providence, Hartford). This is 
fairly consistent with the previous forecast with us seeing the 
risk for localized flash flooding; however, it is not widespread
enough of a threat to warrant a Flood Watch for portions of 
southern New England. 

For timing, this will primarily be and evening and overnight event 
into the early morning hours of Wednesday. Depending on the timing 
of these shortwaves showers/storms could develop may develop as 
early as late afternoon; however, chances increase for the evening 
and overnight timeframe. 

KEY MESSAGE 2...Scattered thunderstorms possible later Wednesday,
but will be dependent on degree of clearing during the day.

Rain continues through the early morning hours of Wednesday. There 
is some question on when the bulk of the rain exits and the coverage 
of showers. Most model guidance has the bulk of rain out by late 
morning; however, there is more spread on the degree of "clearing" 
in the afternoon. If there are lingering showers, as some guidance 
suggests, the suppressed heating will likely end up lowering the 
risk of storms later in the day. If we get enough of a window with 
clearing or breaks in the clouds, instability will be sufficient to 
support thunderstorms developing ahead of a cold front with values 
1000-1800 J/kg of SBCAPE. Moisture won't be as anomalous as the 
previous evening through the whole column; however, the HREF has 
been keen on another surge of higher dewpoint air ahead of the 
front. Across the individual CAMs, there is plenty of spread with 
regards to the timing, coverage, and intensity of convection (if 
any). A couple hint at the potential for scattered showers and 
thunderstorms developing after mid-afternoon moving eastward into
